document.title: Non-Adaptive Cryptanalytic Time-Space Lower Bounds via a Shearer-like Inequality for Permutations

candidate.title: Discrete Logarithm with Preprocessing and r Rounds of Adaptivity
candidate.subtitle: Interpolating between the non-adaptive and fully adaptive time-space tradeoffs
candidate.one_line: An (S,T)-algorithm for generic discrete logarithm with r rounds of adaptivity succeeds with probability at most O~(T^2/N + rST/N).
candidate.informal: An attacker allowed unlimited precomputation on a group, then S bits of notes and T online queries, can compute discrete logarithms far better than one who cannot precompute -- but only if its queries may react to each other. With all queries fixed in advance, the source paper shows preprocessing buys nothing beyond baby-step giant-step; with fully adaptive queries the known algorithms achieve ST^2 = N. This conjecture is the formula in between: with r rounds of adaptivity the success probability should be about T^2/N + rST/N, which recovers both endpoints and is matched at every r by an attack building T/r chains of length r.
candidate.status_note: Open for every 1 < r < T. The r = 1 case is the source's Theorem 1.1 and the r = T case is the bound of Corrigan-Gibbs and Kogan; nothing in between is proved. The source states the interpolation as a conjecture and says it would be sharp.
candidate.progress_note: The matching attack exists for every r: a variant of the adaptive algorithm of [BL13, CK18, Mih10] that builds multiple chains of length r instead of one chain of length T. The missing half is the lower bound, and the source says its Shearer-like inequality cannot reach it.

candidate.why_interesting: It replaces a binary fact -- adaptive algorithms are stronger -- with a quantitative one, and would say exactly how much sequentiality a Pollard-style attack really needs. Both endpoints are theorems, which is rare for a conjecture of this shape.
candidate.why_clean: The bound is an explicit formula, the model is the source's own, and the matching attack is described in one line, so the conjecture is a lower bound with a known upper bound to meet.
candidate.risks: The definition of 'r rounds of adaptivity' is this page's, not the source's -- the phrase occurs once in the paper and is never defined. Check the batching notion in Definition 3 against the two endpoints the source names; any definition that gets r = 1 and r = T right is close to it, but the intermediate content depends on details such as whether batch sizes may adapt.
candidate.formal_statement_latex: There is a function $c(\cdot)$, polylogarithmic in $N$, such that for every prime $N$, every $1 \le r \le T$ and every $(S,T)$-algorithm for DLOG in the generic group model over a group of order $N$ having $r$ rounds of adaptivity, the success probability is at most $c(N) \cdot (T^{2}/N + rST/N)$.

verify.reason: The conjecture is printed verbatim in the source's open-problems paragraph on printed p. 10 (PDF p. 11), with both endpoints identified by the source itself and a matching attack sketched. It is not proved anywhere in the paper: the numbered results are Theorems 1.1-1.3 and 4.1, none about intermediate r. The correction that mattered: the source never defines 'r rounds of adaptivity', so the page had to supply a definition, and the first draft presented it as if it were the source's.

checks.name: existence
checks.finding: Printed verbatim: 'For the DLOG problem, we conjecture that the success probability of an (S, T )-algorithm with r rounds of adaptivity is at most O~(T^2/N + rST/N)'.

checks.name: openness
checks.finding: Stated in a paragraph headed 'Open problems'. The paper proves only r = 1 (Theorem 1.1, printed p. 4) and cites [CK18] for r = T. No result addresses intermediate r; checked against the full list of numbered statements.

checks.name: strength
checks.finding: The source's phrase 'r rounds of adaptivity' is undefined in the paper -- it appears exactly once. The statement therefore depends on a definition the page supplies, which is a change in kind, not degree. Corrected by labelling Definition 3 as the page's own and by pinning it to the two endpoints the source names.

checks.name: quantifiers-and-parameters
checks.finding: The polylogarithmic factor is the source's O~; r ranges over 1..T as the source's 'for any 1 <= r <= T' has it; N prime as in Theorem 1.1.

checks.name: attribution
checks.finding: The conjecture is the source's own. The r = T endpoint is attributed to [CK18] and the matching attack to [BL13, CK18, Mih10], as the source attributes them.

checks.name: definitions
checks.finding: Non-adaptivity is quoted from the source's Section 3.2 (PDF p. 17). The r-round notion is not in the source. Flagged in risks and on the page.

checks.name: fabrication
checks.finding: The obstruction paragraph is the source's own account, quoted. The claim that each extra round buys a factor only in the ST/N term is a reading of the printed formula, labelled as such.

checks.name: self-containment
checks.finding: The generic group model, the (S,T) model and the r-round notion are all on the page; the statement needs nothing else.

corrections.problem: The r-round notion was presented without saying the source never defines it.
corrections.corrected: Label Definition 3 as this page's, and add the remark showing it reproduces the source's two named endpoints.

corrections.problem: The polylogarithmic factor was written as O~ inside the statement.
corrections.corrected: Existentially quantify an explicit polylogarithmic function c(N), so the statement is a proposition rather than an asymptotic idiom.

rejected_in_this_paper.what: Proving time-space lower bounds for adaptive attacks with preprocessing for the other problems the paper treats -- square-DDH and Even-Mansour -- as a function of the number of adaptivity rounds (printed p. 10).
rejected_in_this_paper.why: The source poses the r-round goal 'for the problems considered in this paper' but names a conjectured formula only for DLOG and, separately, an improved bound for DDH. For sqDDH and EM there is no proposition to publish, only the goal.

rejected_in_this_paper.what: Extending the proof technique to challenge-dependent pre-translated queries (printed p. 10).
rejected_in_this_paper.why: A technique-development goal, not a proposition: the source says it 'would require new Shearer-type inequalities or alternative techniques'. It is recorded as the obstruction on c/0060 instead.

rejected_in_this_paper.what: Proving slightly super-linear time-space lower bounds for oblivious branching programs, which the source says its motivating question is related to (printed p. 4, footnote 2).
rejected_in_this_paper.why: A 30-year-old open problem in complexity theory that the source cites rather than poses, attributed to the line of work after Babai-Nisan-Szegedy. Not this paper's to leave open.
